nameStory: The Great Blue Skimmer gets its name from two key traits: its impressive size among the skimmer dragonflies and the stunning blue coloration that mature adults develop. The word 'skimmer' refers to how these dragonflies hunt by skimming low over water surfaces, snatching up mosquitoes and other small flying insects with their basket-like legs.
description: The Great Blue Skimmer is one of New England's largest and most impressive dragonflies, reaching up to 2.5 inches long with a robust, powerful build. Young skimmers start life wearing brown colors, but as they mature, males transform into gorgeous blue beauties with a metallic sheen that catches the sunlight. These are chunky, substantial dragonflies that look like they mean business as they patrol their territories over ponds and lakes. Their wide wings and thick bodies give them a commanding presence among the smaller dragonflies you'll typically see.

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Large and robust dragonfly, noticeably bigger and chunkier than most other skimmers, with broad wings that span impressively when spread

idTips.label: Male Coloration
idTips.description: Mature males develop a striking metallic blue body that can appear almost electric in bright sunlight, with a powdery blue coating called pruinescence

idTips.label: Juvenile Appearance
idTips.description: Young individuals and females are brown with yellow markings, lacking any blue coloration but still maintaining the characteristic large, sturdy build

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Clear wings with dark veining and small amber patches at the base, no distinctive spots or bands like many other skimmer species

idTips.label: Flight Behavior
idTips.description: Strong, purposeful flight with frequent hovering over open water, often returning to the same perch repeatedly like a feathered hawk

habitat: Look for Great Blue Skimmers around larger bodies of still or slow-moving water including ponds, lakes, marshes, and lazy streams with muddy or sandy bottoms. They prefer areas with some open water for hunting but also appreciate nearby vegetation like cattails, sedges, or overhanging branches for perching. You'll often find them in the same spots as painted turtles and great blue herons, who also favor these calm, productive waters.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their aquatic nymph stage in late spring, with brown juvenile forms appearing first around pond edges in May.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs during summer months when mature blue males establish territories and patrol their chosen waters, best spotted on warm, sunny days from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases significantly in early fall as adults die off after mating and egg-laying, with few individuals surviving past September.
seasonality.winter: No adults visible; juvenile nymphs spend winter underwater in pond mud, growing slowly until they're ready to emerge as winged adults next spring.

funFact: Great Blue Skimmers can actually change the angle of each of their four wings independently, making them incredibly agile aerial hunters that can catch prey while flying backwards or hovering in place like tiny helicopters!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other large blue dragonflies, but the Great Blue Skimmer's hefty build and solid blue coloration (without spots or bands) sets it apart. Remember: if it's big, blue, and built like a dragonfly bodybuilder, you've found your Great Blue Skimmer!
contextualKnowledge: The dramatic color change from brown juvenile to blue adult is so striking that early naturalists sometimes thought they were looking at completely different species. This transformation happens as the dragonfly matures sexually, with the blue coloration serving as a signal to potential mates and rivals.
compareHints: Among its Libellula cousins, the Great Blue Skimmer stands out for its large size and solid blue coloration without distinctive wing patterns. The Twelve-spotted Skimmer has obvious white and dark wing patches, the Widow Skimmer shows bold black and white wing bands, and the Spangled Skimmer has a more delicate build with spotted wing tips. Think of the Great Blue as the 'plain but powerful' member of the skimmer family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Libellula cousins, the widow skimmer's wing bands are by far the boldest and most extensive - twelve-spotted skimmers have distinct spots rather than bands, while slaty skimmers lack the dramatic black markings entirely.

Among New England's skimmer species, mature male Slaty Skimmers are distinguished by their uniform slate-blue coloration, unlike the bold white patches of Widow Skimmers or the spotted wings of Twelve-spotted Skimmers.

Among its Libellula relatives, twelve-spotted skimmer is unique in having exactly three spots per wing - four-spotted has one large spot per wing, while widow skimmer has broad dark bands rather than distinct spots.

Among New England's Libellula skimmers, male Spangled Skimmers are the only ones with solid metallic blue coloring - Great Blue Skimmers have blue abdomens but different thorax colors, while Slaty Skimmers are more gray-blue.

Among its skimmer relatives, the four-spotted is distinguished by having the fewest and most clearly defined wing markings - just four bold spots compared to the twelve-spotted skimmer's busy pattern or the widow skimmer's broad white patches.

Among its Libellula cousins, the Painted Skimmer is unique for having amber coloring at both wing bases AND tips - the Twelve-spotted has clear wings with dark spots, the Widow Skimmer has dark bases but clear tips, and the Four-spotted has amber only at the wing bases.
Among its Libellula cousins, the Golden-winged Skimmer's amber wing patches set it apart from most relatives.
Among its Libellula relatives, Needham's Skimmer is distinguished by having dark wing bases without the white patches of Widow Skimmers or the multiple spots of Twelve-spotted Skimmers.
